Items.Authors: Scott Ryan, Thomas Gansheimer, William Goble, Andrew Cline, William Podgorski
Items.Title: A plan for decommissioning HectoSpec and installing ViaSpec hardware at the MMT Observatory
Items.Abstract: The MMT Observatory is planning the complex transition from its legacy HectoSpec & HectoChelle multi-object spectrographs (commissioned 2004) to the new 600-fiber ViaSpec instrument, which will enable a major Milky Way survey. Decommissioning Hecto begins in spring 2026 and focuses on safe removal, avoiding the exterior wall removals and unsafe methods of the original installation. The revised logistical plan involves systematic disassembly, cutting of the optical benches into manageable pieces, and using an interior hoisting system. Subsequent installation of ViaSpec, which includes a fiber positioner, 25-m fiber chain, and a new optical bench, requires reverse logistics and extensive mechanical modifications to the bench room for advanced thermal stability infrastructure. This work details the systems engineering and logistical strategy for executing this critical large-scale instrument replacement.

Items.Authors: Xuejun Zhang, Frank U. Grupp, Long Xiang, Lingtong Zhang, Helena Lamprecht, Hanna Kellermann
Items.Title: A possible telescope for Theon: feasibility study for a 2-meter aperture silicon carbide optical telescope assembly for the Theon mission concept
Items.Abstract: We present a 2 meter Silicon Carbide (SiC) Optical Telescope Assembly (OTA) basic design, hosting an active secondary mirror. We show compliance for this design with the scientific performance requirements of both flavors of the mission: Theon and Theon*. Furthermore, we show that the OTA complies with the ESA M-class mission boundaries with respect to mass, volume, and mechanical loads. The OTA weight, including the active secondary mirror, is projected to be less than 400 kg.  Simulations show that the SiC OTA is strong enough to be launched (in a vertical configuration) on both, an Ariane-6-2 and a Falcon 9 - Block 5 launch vehicle.   We finally link this analysis to a split test concept presented in another paper of this conference, and how this concept allows a cost and time optimized manufacturing sequence, minimizing schedule-related risks. [Grupp, et al. 2026 this conference]

Items.Authors: Martin Prele, Manuel Gonzalez
Items.Title: A rational design methodology for compact rigid-flex interfaces in space instrumentation
Items.Abstract: Rigid–flex interfaces are widely used in space electronics, such as in the Warm Front-End Electronics of the X-IFU instrument on ESA’s ATHENA mission, to decouple connectors from main boards. ECSS constraints on minimum bending radius and transition distance often lead to oversized designs, increasing mass and integration volume. This work presents a physics-based sizing method using Kirchhoff–Cosserat beam theory to predict the deformation of the flexible PCB section under realistic boundary conditions. The model was validated on twelve fabricated boards, showing excellent agreement with measured deflections. Design charts derived from this approach allow rapid optimization of length, height, and clearance, enabling compact, lightweight, and reliable rigid–flex interfaces. This supports better integration of large channel counts in future space-instrument detection chains.

Items.Authors: Erica Sawczynec, Greg Mace, Cynthia Brooks, Daniel Jaffe, Michelle Grigas, Daniel Wilson
Items.Title: A silicon monolithic cross-dispersed grism for mid-resolution near-infrared spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: We report on the process development and manufacturing process for both the high-order entry face and low-order exit face of a silicon monolithic cross-dispersed grism. Additionally, we discuss the preliminary design for a lab prototype medium-resolution (R~10,000) H-band (1.45 – 1.70 um) cross-dispersed grism spectrograph, a proof of concept for future higher-resolution NIR imaging-spectrographs.

Items.Authors: David W. Coutts, Christian Schwab, Tobias Feger, Ali Ghari Zadeh, Ross Zhelem, Sana Syed, Yevgen Kripak, Sameerah Osman, Mark Ferrier, Thomas Walters, Jacob Pember
Items.Title: A simple and effective 3x1 image slicer for coupling into three rectangular fibres
Items.Abstract: Image slicing is an important technique to reconcile large fibre apertures on sky with high resolving power for astronomical spectrometers at medium to large size telescopes. We present a simple and effective image slicer that produces a three by one image slicing configuration, where each slice is coupled into a separate rectangular cross section fibre. A telecentric imaging system is used to produce a magnified image of the fibre output. Two separate mirrors are inserted into opposing sides of the image at approximately 12 degrees to create three separate slices: a straight through central slice, and two singly reflected slices. Each slice is then coupled with its own telecentric imaging system into a rectangular fibre. The whole system is optimised for efficiency.

Items.Authors: Martina Cardillo, Riccardo Campana, Yuri Evangelista
Items.Title: A small, dedicated MeV telescope: the missing capability for identifying galactic cosmic-ray accelerators
Items.Abstract: LHAASO has revealed several Galactic sources emitting up to the PeV range, renewing the search for cosmic-ray PeVatrons. Yet the key 10–100 MeV band, where the pion-decay feature (“pion bump”) offers the clearest evidence of hadronic acceleration, remains essentially unobserved. Several mission concepts covering this range have been proposed but not selected, leaving growing ambiguity in interpreting candidate PeVatrons.    We discuss the motivation for developing a compact, low-cost telescope dedicated to the 10–100 MeV window as a decisive tool to detect the pion bump in candidate PeVatrons sources. A focused mission in this narrow but critical range would provide high-impact science at low cost and offer a unique route to identify the hadronic origin of Galactic cosmic rays.

Items.Authors: Giuseppe Carboni, Andrea Orlati, Sergio Poppi, Carlo Migoni, Matteo Fiorentini, Antonietta Fara
Items.Title: A unified ZeroMQ-based external access layer for DISCOS: real-time telemetry and remote control for the INAF single-dish radio telescopes
Items.Abstract: Modern radio telescopes require flexible and scalable mechanisms to exchange real-time information and support external control. The three INAF single-dish facilities—Sardinia, Medicina, and Noto—are operated through the DISCOS control software, based on the ACS framework. While ACS remains a solid foundation, its CORBA-based and pull-oriented interaction model limits modern third-party applications.  We present a new external access layer for DISCOS that provides message-based, non-blocking interfaces for both real-time telemetry streaming and remote control. The architecture employs a lightweight ZeroMQ messaging layer, combining publish/subscribe channels for state-variable distribution with a complementary request/reply gateway for command execution. This design improves scalability, reduces coupling, and enables a more open and future-proof environment for ACS/DISCOS-based facilities.

Items.Authors: David Hale
Items.Title: A Versatile Camera Interface Platform
Items.Abstract: A modular software platform has been developed to support the control of diverse astronomical camera systems from multiple client types. Although every instrument differs in requirements and capabilities, camera systems generally share a core set of operational workflows. In practice, however, camera control software is routinely re-implemented or adapted from earlier systems, resulting in isolated code bases, duplicated functionality, and limited propagation of bug fixes or improvements.     The presented platform addresses these issues by encapsulating shared functionality in a core set of extensible base modules, with hardware- and instrument-specific logic implemented as replaceable extensions. This architecture reduces duplication, centralizes maintenance, and supports scalable integration. Developed for the Caltech Optical Observatories’ Optical/Infrared Instrumentation group, the platform applies to other astronomical instrumentation environments.

Items.Authors: Haeun Chung, Carlos Vargas, Erika Hamden, Hannah Tanquary
Items.Title: A Web-Based Exposure Time Calculator for the Aspera Far-Ultraviolet Mission
Items.Abstract: We present a web-based exposure time calculator (ETC) developed for the Aspera far-ultraviolet SmallSat mission. Aspera targets extremely faint diffuse O VI emission near 103 to 104 nm, with surface brightness on the order of 1E-18 erg s^-1 cm^-2 arcsec^-2. Accurate S/N modeling is essential for evaluating instrument sensitivity and planning observations. The ETC allows users to compute either the exposure time needed for a desired S/N or the expected S/N for a given integration time. Users can modify spatial binning to explore detectability limits for diffuse emission. The tool implements Aspera’s throughput, detector characteristics, and background estimates in a modular framework and is publicly accessible. This presentation highlights the fundamentals of Aspera ETC framework and its application to other ongoing and future ground and space telescopes.

Items.Authors: Kevin J. Ludwick
Items.Title: Accurately simulating gain and clock-induced charge production in the EMCCD gain register
Items.Abstract: An EMCCD will be used for faint companion detection in the Roman Telescope’s coronograph instrument. As the EM gain increases, the chance of clock-induced charge (CIC) production in the gain register increases, which affects the intended multiplication of charge. I have improved the EMCCD detector simulator used for the Roman Telescope, emccd_detect, so that it accounts for this effect. I demonstrate through maximum likelihood estimation that EMCCD data conform better to the modified probability distribution which accounts for this effect. The use of the modified distribution would in principle improve EMCCD calibration and the accuracy of signal extraction from a frame. I discuss the implementation of this as well as other high-gain phenomena in emccd_detect and demonstrate the enhanced accuracy of the simulator.

Items.Authors: Matteo Tintori
Items.Title: Adaptive optics for the European Solar Telescope: test results of the adaptive secondary prototype
Items.Abstract: The AdOptica Consortium has developed a novel DM prototype that combines high actuator density with low power dissipation, offering a significant technological step forward for solar AO applications. The prototype has a 200 mm aperture with 90 actuators, featuring a reduced pitch that allows finer spatial correction across the wavefront, essential for managing fast-varying daytime turbulence. While improving scalability and energy efficiency, the prototype inherits all the main characteristics of AdOptica’s baseline technology, such large strokes in tip, tilt, and piston, high static accuracy, and the capability to maintain performance even with several inactive actuators—ensuring system robustness and flexibility. It is particularly suited for daytime turbulence compensation with field stabilisation and for use as a post-focal high-order deformable mirror in multi-conjugate AO systems. The paper presents the test results and the wayforward for the EST adaptive secondary final design.

Items.Authors: William J. Marshall, Megan M. Dubay, Thomas Procter, Alan Vasquez Soto, Hank Corbett, Nicholas M. Law, Alex Bucheli, Jonathan Carney, James Dockery, Shannon Fitton, Lawrence Machia, Michael Ronco, Donovan G. Schlekat
Items.Title: ADDem: the Argus deep-field demonstrator
Items.Abstract: This presentation describes the development, commissioning, and autonomous operation of the Argus Deep-field Demonstrator (ADDem), a fully-robotic prototype system designed to characterize the upcoming Argus Array’s ability to co-add frames to achieve deep imaging. The system features six co-pointed 20-cm telescopes, each equipped with a 61-MPix Sony IMX455 CMOS detector, imaging a 9.6 square degree field of view at one minute cadence with 1.4”/pixel sampling. The dataset generated by this instrument over the past year of operation has accelerated Argus pipeline development and enabled scientific projects involving bright transient follow-up and high-cadence solar system object observation.

Items.Authors: Mario Zannoni, Giuseppe Addamo, Oscar A. Peverini, Andrea Limonta, Ludovico Bizzarri, Noemi Mezzanzanica, Mauro Lumia, Giulia Rancati Cattaneo
Items.Title: Additive manufacturing ultralight profiled feed horns for space based sky observations
Items.Abstract: Profiled horn antennas for spaceborne astronomical observations have been prototyped in the 80–170 GHz band using Low Power Bed Fusion on Metal (LPBF/M) technology, enabling the fabrication of lightweight, monolithic metallic structures with highly controlled geometries. The LPBF/M process allows the realisation of optimised horn profiles capable of delivering low return loss, high beam symmetry, and stable broadband performance essential for cosmic microwave background and sub‑millimeter astrophysics missions. Mechanical tests and electromagnetic characterisation confirm that the prototypes maintain structural integrity and optical accuracy under thermal cycling, pre-validating their suitability for space deployment. The flexibility of additive manufacturing also supports rapid design iteration and scalable array production, making LPBF/M a promising pathway for next‑generation high‑frequency focal‑plane architectures in space astronomy.

Items.Authors: Enrico Virgilli, Claire Tonsa, Adriano De Rosa, Carmelo Gargano, Natalia Auricchio, Giovanni De Cesare, Claudio Ferrari, Elena Ferrari, Giuseppe Baldazzi, Riccardo Campana, Ezio Caroli, Marta Civitani, Raffaella Landi, Giuseppe Levi, John B. Stephen
Items.Title: Adjustable gamma-ray optics: active alignment for high-precision Laue lenses
Items.Abstract: Hard X-ray and gamma-ray astronomy above ~70 keV needs focusing optics beyond current capabilities. Laue lenses are the most promising solution, but their development is limited by the challenge of aligning thousands of crystals with arcsecond precision. Adhesive-based mountings introduce angular deviations that exceed requirements. We present “Adjustable Gamma-ray Optics” (AGO), a concept enabling arcsecond alignment and active tuning of each Laue-lens crystal via monolithic flexures actuated by miniature piezo stacks. Each Si(111) crystal is mounted on a tunable lamella, allowing sub-arcsecond Bragg-angle control with minimal area loss. This architecture improves alignment, reduces thermal and mechanical sensitivity, and enables in-flight tuning. A 9-crystal demonstrator with bent crystals, optimized flexures, low-absorption routing, and first alignment strategies validates the approach, paving the way for tunable, high-precision lenses for future missions.

Items.Authors: Matteo Canzari, Thomas Juerges
Items.Title: Adoption and Integration of the IC@MS Alarm Management System within the SKA Control Software
Items.Abstract: The Square Kilometre Array Observatory requires an alarm management solution compatible with its distributed control architecture and IEC 62682 standards. IC@MS was selected for its modular containerised design, native support for Tango Controls alarms, and suitability for large-scale Kubernetes-based operations. Its integration into the SKA software ecosystem involved updating the software to SKA standards, adapting deployment configurations, and migrating the TangoGQL fork to the current upstream version to ensure long-term maintainability. Initial subsystem deployments validated alarm ingestion performance, configuration workflows, role management, and interoperability with existing Tango components. This work marks the first step toward a unified observatory-wide alarm management capability, with further development needed to support full-scale SKA operations and enhanced usability.

Items.Authors: Wim Pessemier, Gert Raskin, Jacob Pember, Jesus Pérez Padilla, Wim De Meester, Maddalena Reggiani, Bart Vandenbussche, Hans Van Winckel, Christian Schwab
Items.Title: Advanced PLC-based control at the heart of the MARVEL telescope array
Items.Abstract: MARVEL is a high-resolution spectrograph fed by four telescopes, currently being commissioned at the Mercator Observatory on La Palma. At the core of the facility's control architecture is a powerful TwinCAT PLC, which not only manages local devices but also coordinates large parts of the entire facility. We highlight the use of industrial vision for fast tip-tilt guiding, the integration of ASCOM/Alpaca devices, and the implementation of a flexible task sequencer for instrument configuration, all on the PLC platform. The system makes extensive use of a web-based TwinCAT HMI for visualizing these features and for rendering basic 3D views of parts of the facility. Additionally, we describe how an improved model-driven code generation framework has enabled us to efficiently deploy fundamental code changes across the system, to migrate decade-old Mercator code to the most recent PLC platforms, and to drastically reduce HMI CPU load by introducing a Model-View-Controller architecture.

Items.Authors: Matteo Canzari, Mauro Dolci, Gaetano Valentini, Fiore De Luise, Amico Di Cianno, Angelo Valentini, Filippo Boschi, Lucio Pacinelli, Nicola Napoleone, Simone Benedetti, Massimo Quintini
Items.Title: Advancing operations at the Campo Imperatore observing station: integrated modernization of telescopes and infrastructure
Items.Abstract: The Campo Imperatore observing station on the Gran Sasso plateau hosts Italy’s highest professional VIS/NIR facility. Two 1-m telescopes, VIT and WOT, are undergoing a coordinated modernization of hardware, control systems, and software infrastructure. VIT is being upgraded with the new CI2RCE InGaAs NIR imager and enhanced control capabilities, while WOT receives updated electronics. Additional developments include site-wide environmental monitoring, extended control hardware, and an integrated software layer for unified operations. This work presents the current configuration of the station and the ongoing refurbishment efforts, aimed at improving reliability, availability, and full remote operability, and outlines the planned return of VIT to scientific operations with its upgraded instrumentation.

Items.Authors: Jorge D. Llop-Sayson, Chaoyin Zhou, Anita M. Fisher, Garreth J. Ruane, Eugene Serabyn, Dimitri P. Mawet
Items.Title: Advancing vector vortex coronagraph technology for the Habitable Worlds Observatory
Items.Abstract: The vortex coronagraph offers an efficient solution to starlight suppression: it provides high starlight suppression while maintaining excellent throughput for off-axis sources. The leading approach to fabricate a vortex coronagraph mask relies on liquid crystal polymers (LCPs), producing what is known as the vector vortex coronagraph (VVC). The main limitation of the VVC arises from mask fabrication errors, which result in a contrast floor above the requirements of HWO. Here, we report recent progress at JPL’s Microdevices Laboratory (MDL) toward fabricating VVC masks for HWO.

Items.Authors: Alyssa Barlis, Stephanie Vivod, Kyle Helson, Sadeq Malakooti, Manuel Quijada, Edward Wollack, Thomas Essinger-Hileman
Items.Title: Aerogels to reduce optical reflections
Items.Abstract: We present initial demonstrations of electromagnetic absorbers to reduce optical reflections fabricated by incorporating carbon particles into polymer aerogel materials. Instruments in the microwave through far-IR are strongly affected by thermal emission from even rather cold surfaces, so careful control of stray light is required to avoid reduced instrument sensitivity. Polymer aerogels offer a unique material system featuring low mass density and index of refraction in addition to tunable optical properties through inclusion of particles. We present the design, fabrication, and characterization of stray-light reduction sheets and molded calibrator targets based on carbon-loaded aerogel material. This technology offers significant improvement in performance (reduced reflectance) as well as lower size and weight compared with current state of the art for stray light reduction or calibrator targets.

Items.Authors: Christophe S. Clergeon
Items.Title: ALTAIR Gemini North SCAO: challenges & performances review
Items.Abstract: ALTAIR, the facility Single-Conjugate Adaptive Optics (SCAO) system for the Gemini North Telescope, has been providing on-sky performance for over twenty years. While Gemini Observatory advances next-generation AO capabilities, High-Strehl ExAO, wide-field LTAO and MOAO concepts, and GLAO facilities, ALTAIR remains a critical asset. Despite the challenges associated with operating and maintaining an aging, first-generation SCAO instrument, it continues to support frontline science on Gemini North. In this contribution, we will present the current status of ALTAIR, outline the operational and technical challenges faced in the context of a maturing AO facility, and describe the ongoing strategy to sustain and enhance SCAO performance at Gemini North during this important transition periode

Items.Authors: John Nijim, Zoran Ninkov, Dmitry Vorobiev, Aditya Kinjawadekar
Items.Title: An application of Hadamard transform spectral imaging (HTSI) to real world data sets and analysis of HTSI optimization techniques
Items.Abstract: Hadamard Transform Spectral Imaging (HTSI) is a signal multiplexing technique used to obtain spectra at every spatial point in the field of view of an instrument, similar to an Integral Field Unit (IFU) spectrograph. The spectra are projected along the rows of a sensing matrix, in this case a Hadamard matrix, by use of multi-slit masks placed at the aperture, which encode the spectra. Taking the inverse Hadamard transform of the resulting observations recovers the spectra. Its main advantage is to provide a signal-to-noise (SNR) increase over direct measurements within the same observation time, where the multiplex advantage is realized. The theory behind HTSI is tested with real world data sets obtained from a laboratory setup and the Southern Astrophysical Research Telescope (SOAR) observatory, and alternative optimal transformations are derived and explored, as well as methods to recover missing data.

Items.Authors: David Hale, Prakriti Gupta
Items.Title: An Improved Waveform Definition Language
Items.Abstract: We present an updated Waveform Definition Language (WDL), a high-level, modular language for defining and compiling detector readout waveforms for CCD, CMOS and hybrid detector systems. Developed for the STA Archon controller and its Archon Configuration File (ACF) format, WDL 2.0 provides a more intuitive, structured syntax that simplifies the creation and maintenance of complex timing patterns. The waveform compiler, significantly improved since our first implementation in 2017, translates symbolic timing rules and parameterized definitions into controller-ready configuration files. Improved error diagnostics and visualization tools enable immediate feedback and waveform timing validation prior to deployment, reducing development and debugging effort.

Items.Authors: Dominic F. Sanchez, Philip Hinz, Renate Kupke, Deno Stelter, Daren Dillon, Cari Johnston
Items.Title: An infrared spectropolarimeter for measuring the 3-micron water-ice feature in protoplanetary disks
Items.Abstract: We present the design of a reflective dispersive Wollaston prism spectropolarimetric mode for the SCALES instrument, enabling simultaneous infrared spectropolarimetry of protoplanetary disks across the 2–4 micron band. The mode provides measurement of orthogonal linear polarization states in a compact configuration compatible with SCALES’ reflective architecture and prism wheel infrastructure. Optical modeling confirms that the reflective double-pass geometry provides sufficient beam separation and spectral coverage across the 3-micron water-ice band, with resolution adequate to resolve the feature. Spectropolarimetric simulations using synthetic data demonstrate sensitivity to scattering-induced polarization, enabling constraints on snow-line location, grain growth, and dust composition.    This work was performed under the auspices of the U.S. Department of Energy by Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory under contract DE-AC52-07NA27344. This document number is LLNL-ABS-2013969.

Items.Authors: Dorian Paillon, Michelle Galloway, Lucia Kleint
Items.Title: An interactive Python simulation for Echelle spectrographs
Items.Abstract: Echelle spectrographs are used worldwide for ground-based astronomy, both nighttime and daytime. Such instruments raise the complexity of an optical design up, mainly adding extra parameters to optimize for one’s science case. I developed an interactive Python simulation dedicated for such goal called SIESTA (Simulating Interactive Echelle Spectroscopy for Targeted Applications). Features include displaying the selected interactive spectral range while showing further information. The need for multiple instances of spectra, simulating multiple spatial elements from an integral-field unit was the main driver behind this new simulation. The scope of my presentation will picture the help and use of this new tool for my current work: designing an integral-field spectropolarimeter for solar physics (Solar Wide-Spectral coverage Polarimeter: SoWiSP), my PhD thesis.

Items.Authors: Briley L. Lewis, Maxwell A. Millar-Blanchaer, Manxuan Zhang, Jayke Nguyen, Max Brodheim
Items.Title: An Open-Source Data Processing Pipeline for NIRC2 Polarimetry
Items.Abstract: The Keck/NIRC2 infrared imager was recently upgraded with a new suite of polarimetric observing modes. This polarimetry upgrade (referred to as NIRC2-Pol) will open up a wide range of new astronomical studies, including investigations of exoplanets, the Galactic center, active galactic nuclei and the solar system. Astronomical polarimeters require sophisticated data reduction, especially for quantitative polarimetry requiring the use of a Mueller Matrix model for instrumental polarization calibration. This work presents a flexible, user-friendly data processing pipeline intended for use with NIRC2-Pol, summarizing its key steps and implementation details. The software is open-source, and written such that it should be straightforwardly adaptable to other dual-channel polarimeters in astronomy, such as Subaru/SCExAO/CHARIS. This presentation will discuss the software infrastructure, with particular emphasis on its adaptability to other astronomical polarimeters.

Items.Authors: Celvi Lisy, Christine Page, Susan Redmond, Saikrishna Manojkumar, Leonid Pogorelyuk, Samantha Hasler, Cheyenne D'Cruz, Garreth Ruane, Niyati Desai, Evana Gizzi, Rebecca Oppenheimer, Chuchu Fan, Kerri Cahoy
Items.Title: Analysis of an augmented extended Kalman filter and convolutional neural network approach for detecting planet signals in dark zone maintenance datasets from the Decadal Survey testbed
Items.Abstract: Direct imaging of exoplanets requires starlight suppression, which can nominally be done using coronagraphs and deformable mirrors. However, starlight suppression is not perfect and residual speckles still challenge traditional post-processing methods. Recent work has shown that AI-based algorithms, particularly Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), can improve exoplanet detection. We extend prior efforts that combined a focal plane wavefront sensor (FPWFS) with an augmented EKF and CNN to detect very dim planets in conditions similar to the Habitable Worlds Observatory. The CNN learns to discriminate noise from injected planetary signals, leveraging drift information captured by the EKF, using the Decadal Survey Testbed. We present the preliminary results and compare performance against traditional high-contrast imaging methods.

Items.Authors: Veronica Baldini, Giorgio Calderone, Igor Coretti, Paolo Cucurullo, Alessandro Marconi, Matteo Porru, Antonio Sulich, Paolo Di Marcantonio, Enrico Pinna, Monica Rainer, Andrea Tozzi, Anna Brucalassi, Marcello Scalera, Chiara Selmi, Alessio Zanutta
Items.Title: ANDES, the high resolution spectrograph for the ELT: control electronics and software for the adaptive optics and integral field units
Items.Abstract: The ANDES (ArmazoNes high Dispersion Echelle Spectrograph) is a second-generation instrument for ESO’s ELT, designed to deliver ultra-stable, high-resolution spectroscopy from the visible to the near-infrared. It will enable breakthrough science, from detecting Earth-like exoplanets to measuring cosmic acceleration. ANDES relies on two key subsystems: the SCAO module, which provides diffraction-limited correction of atmospheric turbulence, and the IFU, which reformats and injects the corrected beam into the spectrograph fiber with high efficiency. This work presents the design of the control electronics and software for both subsystems. The architecture is based on Beckhoff programmable logic controllers (PLCs) integrated within the ELT Instrument Control Framework (IFW), ensuring compliance with ESO standards for communication, synchronization, and safety.

Items.Authors: Edoardo Maria Alberto Redaelli, Nicolò Azzaroli, Chiara Selmi
Items.Title: ANDES, the high-resolution spectrograph for the ELT: SCAO mechanical design and analysis
Items.Abstract: The ANDES instrument has successfully passed the PDR, and the preliminary design of the SCAO subsystem is now consolidated. The single-conjugate adaptive optics module is supported by the front-end subsystem and can be inserted into the optical path by moving a dichroic and a corrector into the beam.  This proceeding presents the mechanical design and the implemented solution, highlighting the design choices and the simulations performed to meet both operational and survival requirements. The hardware selection and the associated budgets are also detailed.

Items.Authors: Giorgio Calderone, Elena Mason, Matteo Porru, Paolo Di Marcantonio, Marco Landoni, Manuel Monteiro
Items.Title: ANDES, the high-resolution spectrograph for the ELT: The star avoidance system
Items.Abstract: ANDES (ArmazoNes high Dispersion Echelle Spectrograph) is the high-resolution, fiber fed spectrograph foreseen  to be installed as a second-generation instrument on the upcoming ELT (Extremely Large Telescope). Equipped  with two movable arms, ANDES is able to simultaneously collect light from the science target and the sky  background, with a sky-projected distance between the fibers 15”≥ d ≥132”. Since there is no field derotator,  the sky background fiber will sample different patches of the sky during an exposure. In this paper we describe  the “ANDES star avoidance” algorithm to automatically calculate the initial position, and the shifts to be applied  on the sky arm during an exposure, to keep it at a safe distance from all possible astrophysical sources and avoid  light contamination.

Items.Authors: Simone D'Auria
Items.Title: ANDES, the high-resolution spectrometer for the ELT: IFU mechanical design and FE analyses
Items.Abstract: ANDES, the high-resolution spectrograph for the ESO ELT, is advancing toward system-level PDR, following the successful Preliminary design review (PDR) of its Integral Field Unit (IFU). This paper reports the setup of the mechanical model used for Finite Element Analysis of the IFU. Starting from the optical design, an initial mechanical layout was produced to evaluate the preliminary opto-mechanical interfaces and structural constraints. The IFU has been decomposed into its main mechanical assemblies and optical mounts to quantify volume, mass, interface loads, and alignment-critical regions. The analysis assesses global and local stiffness, thermal deformation, dynamic response, and seismic resilience, providing input for material selection, mounting strategies, and stability budgeting in preparation for detailed design.

Items.Authors: Ichiro Jikuya, Yoichi Tamura, Akio Taniguchi, Masaki Sakakibara, Akinobu Miyake, Masato Hagimoto, Kianhong Lee, Chihiro Imamura, Shion Takeno, Sachiko Okumura, Nozomi Okada
Items.Title: Anti‑windup PI controller for millimeter-wave adaptive optics: a Nobeyama 45-m radio telescope simulation
Items.Abstract: This work addresses the control problem for Millimeter-wave Adaptive Optics (MAO), which we define as compensating for the optical path length variation between the primary reflector (M1) and the receiver at the focal point. We utilize a measurement system developed by Tamura et al. to track these variations.  The challenge is formalized as an asymptotic constant disturbance rejection problem. We demonstrate that the closed-loop control by an anti-windup proportional-integral (AWPI) controller effectively solves this problem while respecting the physical movement constraints of the optical driving system. Simulation results, based on the Nobeyama 45-m Telescope with a two-axis translating sub-reflector (M2), validate the performance of the proposed AWPI approach. This  approach establishes a foundation for metrology in future large-aperture submillimeter facilities such as AtLAST/LST.

Items.Authors: Dan Sirbu, Rachel Morgan, Ruslan Belikov, Eduardo Bendek, Kevin Fogarty, Jonathan Lin, Kevin Sims, Carson Valdez, Anne Kroo, Olav Solgaard, David A. B. Miller
Items.Title: AstroPIC III: advancing the near-infrared photonic integrated coronagraph for the Habitable Worlds Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), identified as the top priority flagship for astrophysics in the 2020 Decadal Survey, requires a coronagraph instrument reaching ten orders of magnitude starlight suppression to directly image Earth-like planets. Coronagraphs based on Photonic integrated circuits (PICs) offer potentially game-changing advantages for this mission by combining the efficiency and aggressive inner working angles of advanced nulling architectures with the compactness and reconfigurability of integrated photonics.    This third paper in the series provides an overview of technology development efforts for AstroPIC, a near-infrared photonic integrated coronagraph concept for HWO. We review the design and recent high contrast results for AstroPIC, which reached better than 1e-9 contrast ratios with our silicon PIC prototype, including functional system-level demonstrations with a free-space coupling system. We outline the near-infrared science enabled including compati

Items.Authors: Randolph Hammond, John C. Wilson, Stephen A. Smee, Robert H. Barkhouser, Nancy J. Chanover, William Ketzeback, Aidan Gray, Josh Peebles, Stephen Hope
Items.Title: Atmospheric dispersion corrector for the ARC 3.5m telescope
Items.Abstract: We present the design for an Atmospheric Dispersion Corrector (ADC) to be deployed on Nasmyth port 1 (NA1) of the Astrophysical Research Consortium (ARC) 3.5-m Telescope at Apache Point Observatory in New Mexico. The ADC, placed within the NA1 altitude bearing bore, will serve the existing Echelle spectrograph (ARCES) as well as its proposed successor (ASPEN) and require no permanent modifications to the telescope structure. The ADC consists of two, 90mm diameter, counter-rotating prism assemblies. The prisms are mounted within the rotors of servo ring motors, each supported on single 4-point contact thin section ball bearings. Absolute position feedback for the servo motors is provided by magnetic encoders. We will share a detailed system diagram as well as proposed control software architecture designed to interface with telescope operation.

Items.Authors: Victor R. Vestergaard, Viggo R. Fischer
Items.Title: Automated optical SST software and analysis using DTU Space’s Greenland telescope
Items.Abstract: Space Surveillance and Tracking (SST) is essential for maintaining safe and sustainable use of space. DTU Space is currently testing a 50 cm telescope in Greenland to investigate how observations from high latitudes can improve SST. As part of this work, we developed software that automates optical satellite observations and provides initial estimates of their orbits.  The system allows remote control of the telescope and automatically processes images to determine satellite positions. These measurements are then used to compute preliminary orbits. The software performed reliably and produced consistent position data with good precision. Orbit estimation was more challenging due to timing uncertainties, which limited accuracy. The results show promising potential, and ongoing improvements aim to support more accurate SST from Greenland.

Items.Authors: Sydil Kupa, Alex Smith, Sanele Hlabisa
Items.Title: AutoScheduler for MeerKAT observations: a machine learning approach
Items.Abstract: Observations for the MeerKAT Radio Telescope are currently scheduled manually, a slow and error-prone process that limits telescope efficiency. This work applies Machine Learning (ML) to automate scheduling, which is challenging due to astronomical constraints such as Earth’s rotation, horizon visibility, sunrise avoidance, and proximity to the Sun. Large-scale planning is also required because proposals are submitted annually. Three ML approaches are explored: a Genetic Algorithm, AlphaZero, and a heuristic-guided Reinforcement Learning method. Using the Genetic Algorithm, a three-month schedule matching manual results was reproduced, with ML able to schedule about 60% of observations without conflicts and achieving a 30× speedup. A web interface was also developed. Future work aims to reduce clashes and extend scheduling windows.

Items.Authors: Abhay Kumar, Sergio Fabiani, Ettore Del Monte, Giovanni Lombardi, Nicolas De Angelis, CUSP Collaboration
Items.Title: Background modeling for hard X-ray CubeSat polarimeters: case study of the CUSP mission in low-earth orbit
Items.Abstract: The CUbesat Solar Polarimeter (CUSP) project aims to measure the linear polarization of solar flares in hard X-ray band using a Compton scattering polarimeter. CUSP is a project in the framework of the Alcor Program of the Italian Space Agency.  As part of CUSP’s Phase B study, initiated in December 2024, optimizing the signal-to-background ratio is a key objective. In low-Earth orbit, the instrument is exposed to cosmic and albedo X-ray backgrounds, charged particles, and secondary radiation from the spacecraft and atmosphere. Simulating these contributions enables optimization of detector geometry and shielding to maximize signal-to-noise performance. This methodology provides a general framework for future CubeSat missions.    We present initial background estimates for CUSP using a GEANT4-based simulator. A detailed mass model of the CUSP has been implemented to simulate background components and different classes of solar flares to optimize the signal-to-background ratio.

Items.Authors: Edoardo Bellone de Grecis, Lorenzo Busoni, Guido Agapito, Alfio Puglisi, Fabio Rossi, Marco Bonaglia, Tommaso Lapucci
Items.Title: Bronte: a “single-eye” approach for the validation of MORFEO’s reconstruction & control algorithms
Items.Abstract: We present Bronte, the test facility designed to validate the reconstruction and control algorithms foreseen for MORFEO. We break-down the complex MCAO process into a simpler and sequentially executed SCAO test-bed, equipped with a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM), a SH-WFS and a science camera. This setup simulates MORFEO’s wide field, using a SCAO system with an MMSE+POLC reconstructor, without the need to replicate a system of multiple WFSs and DMs capable of sensing the entire wide field all at once. The test facility essentially reconstructs the wide field MCAO loop within a simplified SCAO test-bed, allowing a practical and step-by-step evaluation of MORFEO’s correction capabilities. This approach allows us to assess the performance and focus on critical aspects of the reconstruction and control algorithms in a controlled environment, without the need to fully replicate the real system.

Items.Authors: Jason E. Williams, Karim Kaismoune, Nicholas P. Konidaris, Christoph Birk, Julia E. Brady, Tyson S. Hare, Daniel Kelson, Gerrad Killion, Andrew B. Newman, Gwen C. Rudie, William Schoenell, Johanna K. Teske
Items.Title: Buffered-readout characterization of the H2RG infrared array for the Henrietta spectrograph
Items.Abstract: At the slow pixel rates typical in infrared astronomy (<500 kHz), H2RG infrared sensors can be readout in two ways - unbuffered or buffered. In general, unbuffered readout increases dynamic range and simplifies the external electronics at the cost of increased pixel-to-pixel crosstalk and reduced analog settling time. Conversely, buffered mode reduces the dynamic range and increases the complexity of the readout electronics while suppressing pixel-to-pixel crosstalk and reduced analog settling time. Believing the benefits of buffered readout outweigh the negatives, we present the design of our preamplifier board that drives the H2RG in buffered mode. It features a constant current diode as the current source that drives the output buffer, which enables higher (V/V) gain and linearity. We use this preamplifier board to characterize the H2RG in the Henrietta Spectrograph in terms of gain, linearity, dark current, crosstalk, analog settling time, and read noise.

Items.Authors: Joeleff Fitzsimmons, Krzysztof Caputa, Tim Hardy, Adam B. Johnson, Maaike van Kooten, Olivier Lardière, Christopher Mann, Christian Marois, William Thompson, Jean-Pierre Véran, Jeffrey Chilcote, Saugata Dutt, Darryl Gamroth, Patrick Nkwari, Dmitry Savransky, Suresh Sivanandam
Items.Title: CAL2: assembly and integration of the NRC Canada facility-class focal plane wavefront sensor subsystem into GPI2
Items.Abstract: The direct imaging of exoplanets with existing facility-class adaptive optics (AO) facilities has been fundamentally limited by residual quasi-static speckle noise. The Calibration 2 (CAL2) system for the Gemini Planet Imager 2 (GPI2) upgrade has been designed to overcome this limitation. CAL2 is a National Research Council of Canada (NRC) funded facility-class focal plane wavefront sensor for the GPI2 that employs a self-coherent camera concept and the FAST focal plane mask to perform focal plane wavefront sensing. Using a fraction of the near-infrared (NIR) science bandpass, the CAL2 will be capable of doing science while simultaneously improving the contrast for the GPI2 IFS by up to a factor of 100x on bright stars. The strategies employed and challenges encountered during the assembly and integration of CAL2 into the GPI2 will be discussed and the preliminary results of the focal plane wavefront sensing configuration will be presented.

Items.Authors: Alan Hsu, Jenna Samra, Steven Tomczyk, Daniel Durusky, Jacob Hawthorne, Vanessa Marquez, Abigail Unger
Items.Title: Calibrating the CORSAIR Polarimeter for its Qualification Flight
Items.Abstract: We show results for a probabilistic calibration of the CORSAIR polarimeter. CORSAIR is a new balloon-borne coronagraph and spectropolarimeter that will provide the first uninterrupted observations of the global coronal magnetic field over one month-long solar rotation. We calibrate the polarimeter using a newly developed probabilistic calibration scheme that quantifies the calibration uncertainty explicitly. First, we place a calibration unit in front of the polarimeter to generate known Stokes inputs. Using an infrared source and detector, we project light through the system and record the observed intensities at different modulation states. We model our polarimeter using a probabilistic Mueller matrix framework and estimate the posterior distribution of the free parameters, thus computing the calibration uncertainty in the form of a distribution shift on our initial estimates. We compare our results with existing point-estimate methods used on UCoMP and DKIST.

Items.Authors: Cuán de Barra, Padraig McDermott, Derek O'Callaghan, Alexey Uliyanov, David Murphy, Sheila McBreen
Items.Title: Calibration and characterization campaign of the GIFTS 8U CubeSat gamma-ray detector payload
Items.Abstract: Gamma-Ray Investigation of the Full Transient Sky (GIFTS) is an 8U CubeSat designed to observe and localize GRBs from low-Earth orbit in the Multi-messenger era. Presented here are the results of the extensive characterization campaign for the gamma-ray detector payload performed in UCD which complement and verify Monte Carlo simulations of the detector performance required for GRB localization. Results include the spectral resolution, effective area, and angular response of the GIFTS detectors, as well as calibration functions to convert from detector to energy space. Finally, the results of ground-based testing of GIFTS’ triggering and localization ability are shown, highlighting the mission’s capabilities and importance to the gamma-ray fleet.

Items.Authors: Sarah Steiger, Rémi Soummer, Raphaël Pourcelot, Emiel H. Por, Laurent Pueyo, Iva Laginja, Nathan Scott
Items.Title: Calibration of MEMS DM actuator gains using a Zernike wavefront sensor on the HiCAT testbed and implications for Habitable Worlds Observatory operations
Items.Abstract: Deformable mirrors (DMs) are critical for coronagraph operations on ground-based telescopes and future missions like HWO and Roman CGI. They enable wavefront control to create a high-contrast “dark zone” (DZ) for detecting faint companions. Achieving contrasts <1e-8 requires precise DM actuator-gain calibration, as picometer-level errors degrade DZ digging efficiency, increase overheads, and tighten stability requirements. Because DM gain varies with stroke, rapid in situ recalibration is needed. Zernike wavefront sensors (ZWFS) offer picometer sensitivity and will likely be onboard HWO, but their use for DM calibration remains unproven and has major operational implications. We present HiCAT testbed results calibrating gain maps for two 952-actuator BMC MEMS DMs with both a Fizeau interferometer and a ZWFS. We show that the ZWFS achieves sub-nm sensitivity and supports gain maps using local linear or quadratic models with implications for final DZ contrast and digging efficiency.

Items.Authors: Abhradeep Roy, Yusuke Suda, Yasushi Fukazawa, Norito Nakano, Koume Sakano, Regina Caputo, Daniel P. Violette, Adrien Laviron, Carolyn A. Kierans, Grant Sommer, Jeremy S. Perkins, John W. Mitchell, Lucia Tian, Ryan C. Boggs, Manoj Jadhav, Bobae Kim, Jessica E. Metcalfe, Nicolas Striebig, Richard Leys, Ivan Peric, Hiroyasu Tajima, Shin Kushima, Simon Spannagel, Lennart Huth, Elizaveta Sitnikova, Luca Baldini, Anna Driutti
Items.Title: Characterization and simulation of AstroPix for future space missions
Items.Abstract: Next-generation medium-energy (100 keV–100 MeV) gamma-ray missions require low-power, high-resolution, and highly scalable pixelated detectors. AstroPix, a monolithic HV-CMOS active pixel sensor being developed for the proposed AMEGO-X telescope, aims to meet these needs with ~1.5 mW/cm² power consumption, ~500 µm spatial resolution, 10% energy resolution at 122 keV, and fully depleted silicon layer. A 2×2 AstroPix array, the “quad-chip”, forms a 4×4 cm² module and the basic unit of AMEGO-X’s large-area tracker. We report characterization of the AstroPix v3 quad-chips and introduce A-STEP, a three-layer sounding-rocket payload designed to validate AstroPix in space. We utilized the Geant4-based MEGAlib simulation package to predict event rates, spectra of deposited energy, and reconstruction of the direction of incident particles during the A-STEP flight.

Items.Authors: Claire Tonsa, Enrico Virgilli, Nicolas Barriere, Casper van Aarle, Max Collon, Piero Rosati
Items.Title: Characterization of a silicon-based Laue lens element for future soft gamma-ray modular focusing optics
Items.Abstract: A SiLC (Silicon Laue Component) demonstrator manufactured by cosine (The Netherlands) has been tested at the LARIX facility of the University of Ferrara, Italy. The SiLC focuses X-rays through Bragg diffraction in transmission (Laue) geometry using thin bent silicon plates. Its performance was evaluated with a collimated X-ray beam traveling 26.5 m before reaching the crystal, reproducing astrophysical conditions.  The spatial and energy distributions of the diffracted photons allow us to assess the SiLC focusing capabilities—examining diffraction uniformity along the sagittal curvature and plate alignment—its energy bandpass through meridional curvature, and its peak reflectivity and diffraction efficiency. Experimental results and their comparison with Monte Carlo simulations reproducing the test conditions will be presented.

Items.Authors: Elijah Kane, Peter S. Barry, Chris Benson, Charles (Matt) Bradford, Thomas Brien, Simon Doyle, Victor Gómez-Rivera, Steve Hailey-Dunsheath, Jesús Hernández-Aguilar, José Luis Hérnandez-Rebollar, David H. Hughes, Kirit Karkare, Alex Lapuente, Ryan McGeehan, Raúl Naranjo-Romero, Andreas Papageorgiou, Joseph Redford, Iván Rodríguez Montoya, Sam Rowe, David Sánchez-Arguelles, Sofia Savorgnano, Annie Tan, Marcial Tapia, Jair Vega-Méndez
Items.Title: Characterization of filterbank performance for the SuMAC submillimeter spectrometer
Items.Abstract: The SuperSpec-MUSCAT collaboration (SuMAC) is the joint effort to operate the SuperSpec spectrometer in the MUSCAT cryostat at the Large Millimeter Telescope (LMT). SuperSpec is an on-chip spectrometer developed to greatly reduce the size and thermal mass of a submillimeter spectrometer. SuperSpec uses lithographically patterned filters which couple to kinetic inductance detectors (KIDs) on a silicon chip with an area of only a few square centimeters. The first light of SuMAC took place at the LMT in Summer 2025, with successful observations of submillimeter-bright sources and LIM-style scans. Three polarization-sensitive pixels were deployed, two of which each cover the 190 – 300 GHz atmospheric window, with a moderate spectral resolution of R~200. In this poster, I present the spectral characterization of the filterbanks of the SuMAC instrument, using Fourier-transform and swept-source measurements, as well as full filter bank modeling.

Items.Authors: Kian Syaifoel, Himadri Saha, Felix Münning, Matthias Justen, Netty Honingh, Jochem Baselmans, Dominik Riechers
Items.Title: Characterization of materials and fabrication methods for an MKID filterbank spectrometer for line- intensity mapping of [CII]
Items.Abstract: We are developing an on-chip filterbank spectrometer with the aim of performing line-intensity mapping of [CII] with the CCAT/FYST telescope. We target the 220 GHz - 440 GHz band, with a spectral resolution of R ~ 100. We present the kinetic inductance measurements of our sputtered Al films, which are needed for the design of our MKIDs. We also present our progress in fabrication methods, including a double-resist liftoff method in which we locally control the resist thickness and undercut. We furthermore look into the surface and interface treatments of our samples, in particular with respect to the quality of the NbTiN-Al interface and the sources of TLS noise.

Items.Authors: Simone Pagliarella, Riccardo Ferrazzoli, Paolo Soffitta, Enrico Costa, Alessandro Di Marco, Fabio Muleri, Alessandro Lacerenza, Nicolas De Angelis
Items.Title: Characterization of solar background signatures in IXPE gas pixel detectors through laboratory measurements
Items.Abstract: We present a laboratory–to–flight comparison of the IXPE background signatures, using the spare Detector Unit (DU), identical to the three flight units, exposed to a Co-60 radioactive source, historically adopted as a proxy for solar-induced X-ray background. Co-60 emits 1.17 MeV photons which undergo Compton scattering in the DU structures, producing a degraded spectrum peaking at ~2 keV after ADC counts→keV conversion via Fe-55 (charging measurement) calibration. The source was placed on the top and side of the DU; event tracks were reconstructed to extract spectral and morphological observables (size track, energy fraction in the track’s main cluster, number of pixel hit per event). Lab spectra and parameter distributions are compared with IXPE in-flight in-eclipse (Earth occultating the sun) and in-sun backgrounds from observations. We discuss how the in-flight and on-ground spectral and modulation properties of the background compare to each other.

Items.Authors: Anna K. Gagnebin, Kevin Bundy, Aditya R. Sengupta, Matthew DeMartino, Daren Dillon, Tara Crowe, Caleb Dobias, Stephen S. Eikenberry, Rodrigo Amezcua Correa, Stephanos Yerolatsitis, Holger Schmidt, Avi Patel, Andrew Bradshaw
Items.Title: Characterizing spectral reconstruction performance of a photonic lantern
Items.Abstract: The photonic lantern (PL) is an optical waveguide commonly made by tapering a bundle of single-mode fibers into a multi-mode facet. PLs have been used for coupling multimode light to photonic devices, and more recently for wavefront sensing. By allowing only a single-mode input from a broadband source, the PL – paired with a machine learning spectral reconstruction algorithm – can also be used as a low-resolution spectrometer. Here, we present spectral reconstruction results as a function of the input wavelength in both visible and NIR to assess how deviations from a PL design wavelength of 1550 nm affect performance. We additionally vary spatial characteristics of the input source such as spot location and the angle at which light is injected, as well as the possibility of injecting multiple sources at one time. This work demonstrates a path towards dynamically modulating PL spectrometer systems in order to achieve customized performance in terms of spectral resolution and bandwidth.

Items.Authors: Mingyi Ding, Jing Chen, Liang Wang, Kai Zhang, Jean Louis Lizon, Qiqige Xin, Dinghao Feng
Items.Title: CHORUS on GTC: design and optimization of the exposure meter towards extreme precise radial velocity
Items.Abstract: The CHORUS is a state-of-the-art instrument developed for the 10.4 m GTC telescope in Spain. One of the scientific motivations is to perform the precise radial velocity (PRV) measurement of sub-m/s, to detect habitable rocky planets around solar-type stars, which in turns require an accurate photon-weighted mean time of exposure (MTE) to conduct the barycentric Earth radial velocity (BERV) correction. We simulated the requirements on resolution and frame rate of a chromatic expsure-meter (EXM) operating synchronously with the visiable-band spectrograph (VIS) of CHORUS. Our simulation accounts for the total instrument throughput and variations in atmoshperic conditions, including changes in airmass and thin cloud transient. Finally, we present the optical design of EXM on CHORUS with the optimized configuration, and demonstrated that the MTE calculated with the proposed strategy can fulfill the precision requirement for BERV correction, thereby supporting the PRV science using CHORUS.

Items.Authors: Elana Urbach, Brian Brondel, Franco Colleoni, Felipe Daruich, Erik Dennihy, Ellie Hileman, Petr Kubanek, Fritz Mueller, Douglas R. Neill, Kevin Reil, Mario Rivera, Malhar Sonaniskar, Brian Stalder, Sandrine Thomas, Roberto Tighe
Items.Title: Commissioning and performance of the M1M3 thermal system for the Vera C. Rubin Observatory
Items.Abstract: The M1M3 mirror for the Vera C. Rubin Observatory is a cast borosilicate monolith. With its relatively high thermal coefficient of expansion and large variation in thickness across the monolith, the thermal control system is critical. We discuss the commissioning and early performance of the M1M3 thermal system, which involves temperature controlled air entering each honeycomb cell of the mirror through an air nozzle, before returning and being reconditioned by fan coil units. We discuss how we use this system to cool the mirror to one degree below ambient. We also present an analysis of thermal gradients in the glass measured with 146 thermocouples in the glass, and show progress in mitigating the gradients as we work to reduce both thermal distortion and mirror seeing.
